settings.heading: He Isn't Just Barking At The Window.
settings.heading_hl: Sometimes The Real Trouble Starts In His Gut
settings.text: Many owners of window-barkers, doorbell-reactors and dogs who can't settle notice something else too: scooting, paw licking, loose stools or pacing at 3AM. Those are gut signs — and they're worth a closer look.

settings.heading: Why a dog who patrols the window may not just be “territorial”
settings.text:
A dog who scans the street all day isn't always guarding the house. Sometimes he's simply a dog who doesn't feel right — and a dog who doesn't feel right finds it much harder to switch off.

That's why the curtains help a little, the white noise helps a little, and the training helps with the habit… but the restlessness keeps coming back.

Training can teach him what to do instead. It can't change how he feels.
settings.image_hint: a dog watching out of the window
settings.btn: So what could he be feeling?

settings.heading: Around 90% of the body's serotonin is made in the gut, not the brain
settings.text:
Serotonin is one of the body's main “feel-calm” messengers — and in mammals, the vast majority of it is produced in the gut.

Scientists are still learning exactly how the gut and the brain talk to each other (the “gut–brain axis”), but it's one reason a growing number of vets look at digestion when a dog can't settle.

And the gut is exactly where intestinal parasites live. They're more common than most owners think: a 2020 study found intestinal parasites at 85% of U.S. dog parks tested. Because many parasites shed eggs on and off, a single stool test can come back clear even when something is there.

settings.heading: Sound familiar?
settings.intro: If you recognise three or more of these, your dog may fit a pattern that training alone keeps missing:
settings.items:
He patrols the window and reacts to every car, delivery and passer-by
The doorbell sets him off and he keeps going long after it stops
You can't take a phone call without him getting worked up
You've closed the curtains, tried white noise or moved where you work
He licks his paws at night
He scoots
His coat has gone flat or dull
He paces at three in the morning
settings.outro: The last four are gut signs. If the barking were only about what's outside, they wouldn't be on the list.

settings.heading: Quieting the alarm vs. looking at what's behind it
settings.text:
Calming chews and CBD can take the edge off — for a few hours. That's not because they're fake. It's because they work on the nervous system, not on the gut.

A complete gut routine does three things, every day:

  1. Support the body against parasites at every life stage. Black walnut hull, wormwood root (carefully limited to 0.85% thujone), clove and pumpkin seed.
  2. Keep the gut calm while it works. Marshmallow root, ginger and fennel soothe digestion; Oregon grape root, olive leaf and goldenrod help keep things in balance.
  3. Rebuild healthy gut flora. A four-strain probiotic blend: L. plantarum, L. acidophilus, B. lactis and L. reuteri.

PawGuard Parasite Cleanse Drops bring all 11 actives together in one duck-flavoured liquid — third-party tested and made in a GMP-certified facility. Add it to his food once a day, dosed by weight with the marked dropper. That's the whole routine.
